Academy as an Office Within the Office in the Department

Academy as an office within the Department of Transportation
with the Superintendent as head of Office and reporting directly to
the Secretary of Transportation. E:\HR\OC\HR698.XXX HR698

SUBTITLE C—OTHER MATTERS
Sec. 3521—Limitation on Waiver of Navigation and Vessel-

provisions.heading: Inspection Laws to Address Foreign Entities of Concern
provisions.text:
This section would amend section 501 of title 46, United States
Code, to limit the operation of a vessel under a waiver until the
owner or operator submits to the Maritime Administrator, and the
Maritime Administrator confirms, sufficient proof that the vessel is
not owned, operated, or crewed by a foreign entity of concern as de-
fined in section 10612 of the CHIPS Act of 2022 (Public Law 117–
62).
Sec. 3522—Financing of Fishing Vessels
This section would improve and update the Federal Ship Financ-
ing Program by making construction of new commercial fishing
vessels in the United States eligible under the statute in chapter
537 of title 46, United States Code.
Sec. 3523—Cranes; Shore Power
This section would amend the Port Infrastructure Development
Program to make upgrading cranes at U.S. port facilities, including
updating associated software, eligible for funding under the stat-
ute. Port cranes and associated software made in the Peoples Re-
public of China are a security risk and amending section 54301 of
title 46, United States Code, will help expedite addressing a critical
supply chain vulnerability. This section also makes shore power in-
frastructure projects that support cargo and passenger vessels eligi-
ble for funding under the program.
Sec. 3524—Cargoes Procured, Furnished, or Financed by United

provisions.heading: States Government
provisions.text:
This section would support the commercial U.S. flag fleet by ex-
panding the pool of government cargoes subject to requirements
stipulated in section 55305 of title 46, United States Code.
Sec. 3525—Assistance for Small Shipyards
This section would amend section 54101 of title 46, United States
Code, to clarify that commercially available digital manufacturing
hardware and software products used in the design, construction,
and maintenance of, and digital tools and platforms that can train
workers in shipbuilding skills, are eligible for funding under the
Assistance for Small Shipyards program.

Sec. 3527—Assessment of Channel Depths and Placement of Aids
to Navigation
This section would require the President to provide the relevant
committees with a plan detailing how the U.S. Army Corps of Engi-

the U.S. Coast Guard will improve coordination amongst each other
in making available information on depths, real time physical

Sec. 3528—Waiver
This section would amend section 501 of title 46, United States
Code, to make clear the Secretary of Defense shall provide as part
of a Submittal of Explanation to Congress the waiver issued using
this authority.
Sec. 3529—National Maritime Workforce Advisory Committee
This section would amend chapter 151 of title 46, United States
Code, to establish a National Workforce Advisory Committee com-
prised of not more than 25 representatives of the maritime indus-
trial base workforce. The Committee would advise the Secretary of
Transportation on matters related to the skills, training, and num-
bers of workers necessary to maintain the U.S. maritime industrial
base workforce ashore and afloat. This section would also identify
the categories of experience and expertise that shall be represented
on National Maritime Workforce Advisory Committee.
Sec. 3530—Enhancing United States Maritime Workforce
This section would require the President to submit to relevant
committees proposals to implement workforce provisions from the
Maritime Action Plan issued by the White House.
Sec. 3531—Enhancing United States Shipyards and Shipbuilding
This section would require the President to submit proposals to
the relevant congressional committees to implement recommenda-
tions related to domestic shipbuilding included in the Maritime Ac-
tion Plan issued by the White House.

Sec. 3603—Assessment of the Use of Commercial Best Practices for

provisions.heading: Navy Shipbuilding
provisions.text:
This section would require the Secretary of the Navy in coordina-
tion with the Secretary of Transportation and the Secretary of the
department in which the Coast Guard is operating to conduct an
assessment of best practices for ship construction and repair as
well as identify opportunities for the Navy and Coast Guard to le-
verage those best practices.
Sec. 3604—Military Sealift Command
This section would authorize the Secretary of the Navy to offer
Government merchant mariners employed by Military Sealift Com-
mand paid leave accrual at a faster rate than provided pursuant
to the standard General Schedule system. Additionally, this section
would require a report from the Secretary of the Navy on recruiting
and retention efforts for government civilian mariners.
Sec. 3605—Assessment on Maritime Infrastructure Readiness
This section would require the Maritime Administrator to submit
a report to the appropriate congressional committees on the status,
resources, and authorities needed to complete maritime infrastruc-
ture improvements in the interest of national security and the com-
merce of the United States.
Sec. 3606—United States Merchant Marine Academy

provisions.heading: Infrastructure and Facilities Modernization
provisions.text:
This section would express findings that the United States Mer-
chant Marine Academy, as one of the five Federal service acad-
emies, plays a critical role in training service-obligated licensed
merchant mariners needed for national security and economic in-
terests of the United States. It would further express a finding that
the infrastructure at the United States Merchant Marine Academy
has not been modernized and rehabilitating the campus infrastruc-
ture is necessary to support current and future generations of Mid-
shipmen.
Sec. 3607—United States Merchant Marine Academy
This section would express the sense of Congress about the im-
portance of the United States Merchant Marine Academy, the need E:\HR\OC\HR698.XXX HR698

for sufficient funding for campus infrastructure modernization, and
the importance of rotational presidential attendance at graduation.
Additionally, this section would require a report on the resources
required to increase enrollment at the United States Merchant Ma-
rine Academy.
Sec. 3608—State Maritime Academies
This section would require the Maritime Administrator to submit
a report to Congress detailing the additional resources required to
support increased enrollment at the State maritime academies. The
required report would also assess whether there is a need for addi-
tional State maritime academies.
Sec. 3609—Enforcement of Service Obligation Requirements
This section would require the Maritime Administrator to ensure
that each cadet that signs a commitment agreement at the United
States Merchant Marine Academy and each individual that signs
a student incentive payment agreement at a State maritime acad-
emy meets service obligation requirements of those agreements.
Additionally, this section would require the Maritime Adminis-
trator to establish an electronic system to support individuals
meeting their service obligations and notify individuals if they are
in violation. Not later than 180 days after the date of enactment
of this Act, and annually thereafter, the Maritime Administrator
would be required to submit a report to Congress on the status of
all service-obligated mariners.
Sec. 3610—State Maritime Academy Sea Term Scholarship
Programs
This section would amend chapter 515 of title 46, United States
Code, to add a new section that would require the Maritime Ad-
ministrator to work with private entities in the maritime industry
to establish a sea term scholarship program.
Sec. 3611—Implementation Plan
This section would require the Maritime Administrator and the
Secretary of the department in which the Coast Guard is operating
to each submit an implementation plan of the sections in this title
and provide a briefing to the appropriate congressional committees
on the implementation plans. Additionally, this section would re-
quire biannual updates on the implementation of such plans and
a comptroller general review of the efforts carried out pursuant to
this title.

HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES,
COMMITTEE ON APPROPRIATIONS,
Washington, DC, June 11, 2026.
Hon. MIKE ROGERS,
Chairman, Committee on Armed Services,
House of Representatives, Washington, DC.
DEAR CHAIRMAN ROGERS: I am writing to you concerning H.R.
8800, the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027.
There are certain provisions in the legislation that fall within the
Rule X jurisdiction of the Committee on Appropriations.
In the interest of permitting your committee to proceed expedi-
tiously to floor consideration of this important bill, I am willing to
waive this committee’s right to sequential referral. I do so with the
understanding that by waiving consideration of the bill, the Com-
mittee on Appropriations does not waive any future jurisdictional
claim over the subject matters contained in the bill that fall within
its Rule X jurisdiction. I request that you urge the Speaker to
name members of this committee to any conference committee that
is named to consider such provisions.
Please place this letter in the committee report on H.R. 8800 and
in the Congressional Record during consideration of the measure
on the House floor. Thank you for the cooperative spirit in which
you have worked regarding this matter and others between our re-
spective committees.
Sincerely,
TOM COLE,
Chairman. E:\HR\OC\HR698.XXX HR698

provisions.heading: CONGRESSIONAL BUDGET OFFICE ESTIMATE
provisions.text:
In compliance with clause 3(c)(3) of rule XIII of the House of
Representatives, the cost estimate prepared by the Congressional
Budget Office and submitted pursuant to section 402 of the Con-
gressional Budget Act of 1974 is as follows:
JUNE 11, 2026.
Re: Direct Spending and Revenue Effects of H.R. 8800, the Na-
tional Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027
Hon. MIKE ROGERS,
Chairman, Committee on Armed Services,
House of Representatives, Washington, DC.
DEAR MR. CHAIRMAN: The Congressional Budget Office has com-
pleted an estimate of the direct spending and revenue effects of

provisions.heading: H.R. 8800, the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year
provisions.text:
2027, as ordered reported by the House Committee on Armed Serv-
ices on June 4, 2026. This estimate is based on the Committee
Print 119–33, which was posted to the website of the House Com-
mittee on Rules on June 11, 2026.
Enacting the bill would have an insignificant net effect on direct
spending and revenues each year and in total over the 2027–2036
period, CBO estimates. Provisions that would affect direct spending
and revenues include the following:
• Some provisions in H.R. 8800 would affect direct spending
by between ¥$500,000 and $500,000, generally because very
few people would be affected. Those provisions primarily in-
volve personnel benefits such as health care and compensation.
• Several provisions would allow the Department of Defense
to collect receipts (which are recorded as reductions in direct
spending) and spend them without further appropriation so
that the net effect on direct spending would be negligible.
• Four sections would modify the authority of working cap-
ital funds to incur obligations in advance of appropriations,
which is classified as direct spending. CBO estimates that the E:\HR\OC\HR698.XXX HR698
GNIRAEH

net change in spending for those provisions would be between
¥$500,000 and $500,000.
• Five sections would increase revenues from criminal fines
by less than $500,000.
Because the bill would affect direct spending and revenues, stat-
utory pay-as-you-go procedures apply.
CBO estimates that enacting H.R. 8800 would not increase net
direct spending by more than $2.5 billion in any of the four con-
secutive 10-year periods beginning in 2037.
CBO estimates that enacting H.R. 8800 would not increase on-
budget deficits by more than $5 billion in any of the four consecu-
tive 10-year periods beginning in 2037.
Our complete cost estimate for H.R. 8800, including a discussion
of discretionary authorizations and mandates under the Unfunded
Mandates Reform Act, will be provided as soon as it is available.
I hope this information is useful to you. If you wish further de-
tails on this analysis, we would be pleased to provide them.
Sincerely,
PHILLIP L. SWAGEL,
Director.

provisions.heading: GENERAL PERFORMANCE GOALS AND OBJECTIVES
provisions.text:
With respect to clause 3(c)(4) of rule XIII of the Rules of the
House of Representatives, the general goals and objectives of H.R.
8800 are to maintain the national defense, to prepare the United
States to meet current and future challenges to the national de-
fense, and to accomplish each of those goals and objectives in a re-
sponsible manner.
The bill authorizes $1.14 trillion of discretionary funding to sup-
port national defense requirements. The bill authorizes funding
sufficient to provide a 5 to 7 percent pay raise for servicemembers,
to invest in key maintenance and readiness areas, and to mod-
ernize the force to deter adversaries.
The bill continues the longstanding work of the Committee on
Armed Services to provide U.S. military forces with sufficient re-
sources to maintain the national defense, and it fulfills the commit-
tee’s duties under Article I, Section 8, of the Constitution.

provisions.heading: DUPLICATION OF FEDERAL PROGRAMS
provisions.text:
Pursuant to clause 3(c)(5) of rule XIII, no provision of H.R. 8800
establishes or reauthorizes a program of the Federal Government
known to be duplicative of another Federal program, a program
that was included in any report from the Government Account-
ability Office to Congress pursuant to section 21 of Public Law
111–139, or a program related to a program identified in the most
recent Catalog of Federal Domestic Assistance. E:\HR\OC\HR698.XXX HR698

provisions.heading: COMMITTEE VOTES
provisions.text:
In accordance with clause 3(b) of rule XIII of the Rules of the
House of Representatives, recorded votes were taken with respect
to the committee’s consideration of H.R. 8800. The record of these
votes is contained in the following pages.
The committee ordered H.R. 8800 to be reported to the House
with a favorable recommendation by a vote of 44–12, a quorum
being present.

provisions.heading: RECORDED VOTE NO. 32
provisions.text:
H.R. 8800
On Garamendi Log 6857r1—Repeals the statutory inventory re-
quirement that prohibits reducing the number of U.S. interconti-
nental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) and mandates a Department of
Defense report to evaluate alternative nuclear force compositions
with fewer or entirely off-alert ICBMs.

provisions.heading: ADDITIONAL VIEWS
provisions.text:
Following the passage of this year’s National Defense Authoriza-
tion Act by the House Armed Services Committee, I write to share
my additional views and concerns with the bill as marked up by
the full committee. The National Defense Authorization Act for Fis-
cal Year 2027 authorizes significant investments in our service
members, military families, readiness, military construction, ship-
building, sustainment, and the defense industrial base. I appreciate
the committee’s bipartisan work to provide for the common defense
and to ensure our servicemembers have the support necessary to
carry out their missions.
However, I must register serious concern with the direction of
this bill and the broader defense posture it reflects. The bill
autho1izes a $1.15 trillion defense topline while Congress also
plans to advance another $350 billion in defense spending through
reconciliation, with far too little specificity, accountability, or mean-
ingful oversight. At a time when taxpayers are being asked to sup-
port unprecedented levels of defense spending, it is irresponsible
for Congress to provide the Department with hundreds of billions
of additional dollars while failing to demand basic discipline over
costly nuclear modernization programs, politicization of the Depart-
ment of Defense, and the executive branch’s use of military force
without meaningful congressional authorization. I am also dis-
appointed that the committee failed to adopt basic guardrails for
commercial data centers on milita1y installations. These short-
comings should be corrected before this bill becomes law.

provisions.heading: FISCAL RESPONSIBILITY AND TOPLINE ACCOUNTABILITY
provisions.text:
‘‘An object in motion remains in motion.’’ The term is as true in
government as it is in physics. Year after year, we continue to in-
crease our defense spending, reaching ever-higher levels. Adjusted
for inflation, we are spending an amount roughly equal to what we
spend in 1943. Such high levels are wholly unjustified today, par-
ticularly since this administration continues to claim, however un-
believable it may be, that we are not at war even as it requests
ever larger budgets.
I remain deeply concerned with the defense topline. As this ad-
ministration defunds humanitarian assistance programs, disman-
tles our education system, undermines access to healthcare, and
chips away at hard-earned public benefits in the name of cost sav-
ings, the boulder of defense spending continues to roll down the
hill, picking up speed as it goes, regardless of the damage it may
cause. It is time for Congress to act: to cut wasteful defense spend-
ing, impose meaningful oversight, and reassert its responsibility to
ensure that our defense budget is reasonable, accountable, and
aligned with the needs of the American people.

A larger defense budget, standing alone, is not a strategy. It can
mask mismanagement, reward cost growth, and allow troubled pro-
grams to continue without the discipline that Congress should de-
mand. At a time when families across the country are asked to
make difficult choices, Congress should not authorize enormous de-
fense increases without a clear showing that every dollar is nec-
essary, executable, and tied to real national security outcomes.
However Sisyphean may seem, it’s time for us to push the boul-
der back up the Hill and restore balance. It’s time to restore true
congressional oversight. We cannot keep funding ever larger de-
fense budgets with less oversight and be surprised when the presi-
dent takes advantage of it. The first step to restoring that balance
is for Congress to reclaim its constitutional role: demanding trans-
parency before authorizing new spending, requiring accountability
before expanding failed programs, and insisting that no adminis-
tration, regardless of party, may use the military or the public
purse without meaningful congressional scrutiny.

provisions.heading: OVERSIGHT AND ACCOUNTABILITY WINS
provisions.text:
Although I remain concerned with the overall direction of this
bill, I appreciate that several oversight and accountability provi-
sions were accepted. These provisions do not cure the larger flaws
in the bill, but they are meaningful steps toward better congres-
sional oversight and a more responsible defense enterprise.
I am encouraged that the bill includes important reforms to
strengthen cost-growth accountability, including improvements to
Nunn-McCurdy oversight and additional reporting on NNSA cost-
growth compliance. It also includes F–35 accountability provisions
requiring greater scrutiny of multiyear procurement savings and a
reset plan for the F–35 global sustainment spares backlog. I am
also pleased that the committee accepted provisions related to V–
22 Osprey safety oversight, domestic manufacturing requirements
for shipbuilding programs, limits on Jones Act waivers involving
foreign entities of concern, shipyard workforce concerns, and con-
tractor progress payment protection. I am proud to have joined my
colleagues in adding an amendment that would improve the De-
partments Right to Repair by taking meaningful steps toward im-
proving sustainment oversight, technical-data access, and the De-
partment’s ability to repair and maintain the systems it buys.
These wins should be built upon, not treated as a substitute for the
broader accountability this bill still lacks.
I am proud of my amendment to ensure that the Department of
Defense can hold defense contractors accountable for poor perform-
ance. However, I am concerned that a provision included in the
original bill would have effectively given defense contractors a veto
over their own punishment. Whether the issue is price-gouging,
poor performance, or the misallocation of taxpayer funds, the De-
partment needs more tools to hold contractors accountable, not
fewer.

provisions.heading: NUCLEAR MODERNIZATION
provisions.text:
As I noted in my additional views last year, I continue to have
grave concerns about the direction of the United States’ nuclear en-
terprise. When Congress considers weapons of this destructive E:\HR\OC\HR698.XXX HR698

power, our decisions must be guided by strategic need, fiscal re-
ality, risk reduction, and constitutional oversight. This bill again
fails to demand sufficient scrutiny of nuclear modernization plans
that are growing more expensive, more difficult to execute, and less
clearly connected to today’s security environment.
For another year, the committee declined to provide the Depart-
ment of Defense with flexibility on the statutory requirement to
maintain a fixed number of intercontinental ballistic missiles. A
rigid requirement to keep 400 ICBMs deployed and available is not
a substitute for analysis. It deprives the President and the Depart-
ment of the flexibility needed to adapt nuclear posture to evolving
threats, arms control opportunities, resource constraints, and the
demonstrated survivability of the sea-based and bomber legs of the
triad. Congress should ask what force is necessarily to deter adver-
saries, not preserve an arbitrary number because it has become po-
litically difficult to revisit.

provisions.heading: The Sentinel Intercontinental Ballistic Missile program and the
provisions.text:
plutonium modernization program remain clear examples of why
this oversight is necessary. Sentinel has already experienced ex-
traordinary cost growth and schedule pressure, yet Congress con-
tinues to act as though continuing the program unchanged is the
only acceptable option. NNSA has also repeatedly acknowledged
the difficulty of meeting statutory pit production requirements, and
independent reviews have raised serious concerns about costs,
schedules, and execution. Congress should require credible life-
cycle cost estimates, integrated schedules, and a full comparison of
alternatives, including reuse and refurbishment of existing pits
where technically viable.
I am also concerned by continued support for the nuclear sea-
launched cruise missile, tactical nuclear capabilities, low-yield nu-
clear options, potential nuclear-armed hypersonic systems, explo-
sive nuclear testing, and expansive missile defense concepts that
could increase strategic instability. Congress should focus on reduc-
ing nuclear risks, preserving channels for strategic stability, and
avoiding costly programs that invite arms racing without making
the American people safer. As I wrote in a journal article earlier
this year, ‘‘Congress may have enabled arms races in the past, but
a reinvigorated Congress has the authority and responsibility to re-
duce the risk from nuclear weapons. It’s time we started acting like
it.’’.

provisions.heading: POLITICIZATION OF THE MILITARY AND DEPARTMENT OF WAR
provisions.text:
RENAMING
I strongly object to the committee’s decision to adopt language
deeming references to the Department of Defense and Secretary of
Defense as references to the Department of War and Secretary of
War. The name Department of Defense reflects the proper purpose
of the institution: to defend the United States, uphold the Constitu-
tion, and protect the American people under civilian control.
Changing that name does nothing to improve readiness, strengthen
deterrence, support servicemembers, or repair the defense indus-
trial base.
Instead, this proposal is a costly and disruptive act of political
symbolism. It would create administrative confusion across law, E:\HR\OC\HR698.XXX HR698

tion systems, signage, and official communications. More impor-
tantly, it sends the wrong message about the role of the United
States military. Our military exists to defend the nation, not to

politicization of the armed forces and to preserve the professional,
nonpartisan character of military service.

provisions.heading: MILITARY INSTALLATION NAMES
provisions.text:
By contrast, I was pleased that the Committee adopted language
requiring military installations to be renamed in a manner that
better reflects American values and honors the right people. This
is a modest but important victory. Congress should not allow any
administration to rewrite military history at will, restore honors to
Confederate generals who betrayed the United States, or disregard
the process Congress established to ensure that our military instal-
lations reflect the best of our country.

provisions.heading: DATA CENTERS ON DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE INSTALLATIONS
provisions.text:
I am disappointed that the committee rejected an amendment to
establish basic oversight for commercial data centers on Depart-
ment of Defense installations. Data centers are becoming critical
infrastructure, but they also require enormous amounts of power,
water, land, security, and infrastructure support. When such facili-
ties are placed on or near military installations, Congress has a re-
sponsibility to ensure they do not undermine readiness, training,
installation resilience, or community quality of life.
The amendment would have required the Secretary of Defense to
certify, before entering into an agreement for the construction or
operation of a commercial data center, that the facility had a clear
military purpose and posed no risk to national defense. It would
have required the Department to assess costs, continuity of oper-
ations, energy supply, water consumption, sound and light pollu-
tion, encroachment on training and operations, physical security,
supply chain risks, personnel security, and the ability of sur-
rounding communities to raise concerns. These are not unreason-
able requirements. No installation should be asked to trade readi-
ness, energy resilience, water security, or future mission needs for
opaque commercial arrangements.

provisions.heading: CONGRESSIONAL WAR POWERS
provisions.text:
Finally, I am deeply concerned that this bill does not do enough
to reassert Congress’s constitutional role over decisions to use mili-
tary force. The Constitution gives Congress the power to declare
war, raise and support armies, provide and maintain a navy, make
rules governing the armed forces, and fund military operations. E:\HR\OC\HR698.XXX HR698

These responsibilities are not optional, and they cannot be dele-
gated away because it is politically easier to remain silent.
No administration, of either party, should be permitted to place
servicemembers in harm’s way, risk escalation with foreign powers,
or initiate sustained hostilities without meaningful consultation
with Congress and, when required, explicit authorization. After-
the-fact briefings are not a substitute for congressional authoriza-
tion. This is not a partisan issue; it is a constitutional issue. Our
servicemembers deserve clear legal authority for the missions we
ask them to execute, and the American people deserve a Congress
willing to debate and vote on matters of war and peace.
Our decisions should be guided by careful consideration, constitu-
tional responsibility, and a commitment to spending taxpayer dol-
lars wisely. I will continue to support investments that strengthen
our servicemembers, improve readiness, rebuild the defense indus-
trial base, and protect the United States. But I will also continue
to oppose policies that waste resources, politicize the military, in-
crease nuclear risks, or erode the role of Congress in decisions of
war and peace. We owe it to the American people and to those who
se1ve to get this right.
Sincerely,
JOHN GARAMENDI,
Member of Congress.
